3.3 Bond Pricing

Bond cash flows

Section titled “Bond cash flows”

An ordinary bond promises two kinds of payment: the face value (often 1000 or 100) repaid at maturity, and regular interest payments before maturity, called coupons. The yearly coupon divided by the face value is the coupon rate. For example, a bond with a face value of 1000, a 6% coupon rate, 5 years to maturity and one payment a year pays 60 each year for 5 years and repays 1000 in year 5. US Treasuries and most corporate bonds pay every six months, half of the yearly coupon each time.

So a bond is an annuity plus a single payment at maturity (annuity). At a discount rate yyy, a bond with face value FFF, coupon CCC per period and TTT periods to maturity has the price

P=C×1−(1+y)−Ty+F(1+y)TP = C \times \frac{1 - (1 + y)^{-T}}{y} + \frac{F}{(1 + y)^T}P=C×y1−(1+y)−T​+(1+y)TF​
Check C1
A bond has a 6% coupon rate, and the market requires a 5% yield on it. Its price is:
A bond trades at face value only when its coupon rate equals the required yield. Here they differ.
Does this bond pay more or less each year than a coupon at the required yield would? Would investors pay more or less for it?
The years to maturity affect how far the price is from face value, but not the direction.

Yield to maturity

Section titled “Yield to maturity”

What can be observed in the market is the bond’s price. The discount rate yyy that makes the formula hold is called the yield to maturity (YTM): it is the internal rate of return of buying the bond at its market price.

The formula shows:

  • Price and yield to maturity move in opposite directions: when the yield rises, the present value of future cash flows falls, and the price falls.
  • When the coupon rate equals the yield, the price equals the face value (par); when the coupon rate is above the yield, the price is above face value (premium); when below, the price is below face value (discount).
  • The relation between price and yield is not a straight line but a curve bowed toward the origin: the price rises more when the yield falls than it falls when the yield rises by the same amount (3.4 Interest Rate Risk discusses this convexity).

The yearly coupon divided by the price is called the current yield. It reflects only the coupon, not the movement of the price toward face value, so a premium bond’s current yield is above its yield to maturity and a discount bond’s is below.

Check C2
In Figure 2-1, a 5% coupon, 10-year bond trades at par (yield 5%). Comparing a 1-point fall in yield with a 1-point rise, the size of the price change is:
Look at the shape of the price curve in the figure: is it steeper or flatter on the low-yield side?
The two changes would be equal only if price and yield were related by a straight line. Is it a straight line in the figure?
This bond does trade at par. Think about which way the price curve bends.

How prices change over time

Section titled “How prices change over time”

Even if the yield to maturity does not change, a bond’s price changes over time: at maturity the price must equal face value. So a premium bond’s price falls year by year and a discount bond’s rises, both moving toward face value (pull to par).

If the yield does not change, the holding return for a year (the coupon plus the change in price, divided by the price at the start of the year) equals the yield to maturity exactly: a premium bond pays higher coupons, but part of them is offset each year by the fall in price; a discount bond is the reverse.

But the yield to maturity is not a return the investor is sure to earn: it assumes the bond is held to maturity, the issuer does not default, and all coupons received can be reinvested at the same yield (Exercises Question 5).

Check C3
You buy a 5-year bond at a yield to maturity of 5% and sell it a year later. Even if the market yield has risen to 6% during the year, your holding return for the year is still 5%.
Think: when the market yield rises, what happens to the bond's price? If you sell before maturity, does that affect your holding return?

Zero-coupon bonds and spot rates

Section titled “Zero-coupon bonds and spot rates”

A bond that pays a single amount at maturity, with no coupons in between, is called a zero-coupon bond. It sells below face value, and its whole return comes from the price rising toward face value. Through its STRIPS program, the US Treasury lets each coupon and the principal of a Treasury be separated and traded as separate zero-coupon bonds.

The yield to maturity of a ttt-year zero-coupon bond is called the ttt-year spot rate, written sts_tst​: the yearly return from investing today and receiving a single payment in ttt years.

A coupon bond can be seen as a set of zero-coupon bonds: each cash flow is one zero. So each cash flow should be discounted at the spot rate for its own maturity:

P=∑t=1TCFt(1+st)tP = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\text{CF}_t}{(1 + s_t)^t}P=t=1∑T​(1+st​)tCFt​​

If a coupon bond’s price differs from this value, one can buy the cheap side and sell the expensive side (for example, strip a coupon Treasury and sell the zeros), earning a risk-free arbitrage profit. The yield to maturity replaces all the spot rates with a single discount rate; it is a kind of weighted average of the spot rates. So bonds with the same maturity but different coupon rates can have different yields to maturity even when all are priced from the same spot rates; this is called the coupon effect (Exercises Question 3).

Check C4
The 1-year spot rate is 4% and the 2-year spot rate is 5%. A 2-year coupon Treasury trades below the price obtained by discounting its cash flows at these two spot rates. How can a riskless profit be made?
Shorting the bond means selling the cheap side. Arbitrage buys what is cheap and sells what is expensive.
Just buying and holding earns a higher return but still bears risks such as rate changes, so it is not riskless arbitrage.
Different yields do not prevent arbitrage: what matters is the price of the bond compared with the zeros that replicate it.

Forward rates

Section titled “Forward rates”

Suppose the 1-year spot rate is s1s_1s1​ and the 2-year rate s2s_2s2​. An investor can invest for two years in two ways: buy a 2-year zero directly, or buy a 1-year zero and reinvest for another year when it matures. The rate for the second year under the second plan is not known today, but an “implied” rate that makes the two plans equal can be computed from today’s prices:

(1+s2)2=(1+s1)(1+f1,2)(1 + s_2)^2 = (1 + s_1)(1 + f_{1,2})(1+s2​)2=(1+s1​)(1+f1,2​)

f1,2f_{1,2}f1,2​ is called the forward rate from year 1 to year 2. It is a future rate that can be locked in today: for example, buying a 2-year zero while shorting a 1-year zero amounts to investing for one year from year 1 at f1,2f_{1,2}f1,2​. How forward rates relate to the rates people expect in the future is the subject of 3.5 The Term Structure of Interest Rates.

Check C5
The 1-year spot rate is 4% and the 2-year spot rate is 5%. The rate that can be locked in today with zeros, from year 1 to year 2, is above 5%.
Think: if two years at 5% must give the same result as one year at 4% and one year at some other rate, what must the second-year rate be?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • A bond = an annuity (coupons) + face value at maturity; price P=C×1−(1+y)−Ty+F(1+y)TP = C \times \frac{1 - (1 + y)^{-T}}{y} + \frac{F}{(1 + y)^T}P=C×y1−(1+y)−T​+(1+y)TF​.
  • The yield to maturity is the IRR of buying at the market price; price and yield move inversely along a convex curve. A coupon rate above the yield gives a premium, below it a discount.
  • With an unchanged yield, the price is pulled to par and the holding return equals the yield to maturity; but the yield to maturity assumes holding to maturity, no default and reinvestment of coupons at the same yield.
  • The yield on a zero is a spot rate; each cash flow of a coupon bond should be discounted at the spot rate for its maturity, or there is arbitrage.
  • The forward rate f1,2f_{1,2}f1,2​ satisfies (1+s2)2=(1+s1)(1+f1,2)(1 + s_2)^2 = (1 + s_1)(1 + f_{1,2})(1+s2​)2=(1+s1​)(1+f1,2​) and can be locked in today.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A 10-year US Treasury note has a face value of 100 and a 4% coupon, paying 2 every six months; its quoted yield to maturity is 4.5% (compounded semiannually, so 2.25% per half-year). (a) What is its price? (b) To compare its yield with that of an annual-pay bond quoted with annual compounding, what conversion is needed first?
Question 2 ★
30-year and 2-year zero-coupon bonds with face value 100 both yield 5% (annual compounding). (a) If the yield rises to 6% or falls to 4%, by what percentage does each bond's price change? (b) Why is the price more sensitive to the yield, and the rise and fall more asymmetric, the longer the maturity?
Question 3 ★
Spot rates: 1 year 3%, 2 years 5%, 3 years 6%. Two 3-year Treasuries with face value 100 and annual coupons: L has a 2% coupon and H a 10% coupon. (a) Price both bonds with the spot rates and find their yields to maturity. (b) An investor says "L has the higher yield to maturity, so L is cheaper". Is he right? Why do the two yields differ?
Question 4
The 1-year spot rate is 3% and the 2-year 4%. You want to invest for two years: buy the 2-year zero, or buy the 1-year zero and reinvest for a year after it matures. (a) Above what 1-year rate a year from now is the second plan better? (b) If you think that rate will be 4.5%, which do you choose? What risk does the second plan carry?
Question 5
A bond has face value 1000, a 6% annual coupon and 5 years to maturity. You buy it at 1043.29 (yield to maturity 5%) and hold it to maturity, but coupons can only be reinvested at 3% a year. (a) What is your realized yearly return over the 5 years? (b) Why is it below 5%? Does a zero-coupon bond have this problem?
